1.title: RAG Pipelines: Chunking and Indexing
1.text: Welcome to Module nine: R A G Pipelines: Chunking and Indexing. This module covers r a g pipelines: chunking and indexing. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. The stages of a R A G pipeline and what can go wrong at each. Chunking strategies and sizes. Indexing: embeddings, keyword (B M twenty-five) and hybrid indexes, metadata. Contextual retrieval and freshness management. When not to use R A G.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lumen Advisory Builds a Knowledge Assistant for a Law-Adjacent Compliance Team
1.text: Our running case is Lumen Advisory. Lumen Advisory Builds a Knowledge Assistant for a Law-Adjacent Compliance Team. thirty thousand pages of regulations, internal policies and past rulings, updated weekly. Analysts need cited answers with exact clause numbers. After one weekly refresh the assistant starts giving confident wrong answers.

1.title: The Pipeline
1.text: The Pipeline. The figure shows this: A R A G pipeline: ingest and parse, clean, chunk, enrich, embed and index, retrieve, rerank, generate with citations; an offline indexing half and an online query half.

1.title: The Pipeline, continued
1.text: The Pipeline, continued. Ingest and parse. Purpose: Read P D F s, H T M L, tables. Typical failure: Lost tables, scanned pages, broken order. Clean. Purpose: Remove boilerplate, deduplicate. Typical failure: Repeated headers dominate results. Chunk. Purpose: Split into retrievable units. Typical failure: Chunks too big (diluted) or too small (no context). Enrich. Purpose: Add metadata and context. Typical failure: Missing source, date, section. Embed and index. Purpose: Vectors plus keyword index. Typical failure: Mismatched embeddings; stale index. Retrieve. Purpose: Find candidates. Typical failure: Misses exact identifiers; irrelevant hits. Rerank. Purpose: Reorder by relevance. Typical failure: Skipped; latency added. Generate with citations. Purpose: Answer from the chunks. Typical failure: Unsupported claims; wrong citations.

1.title: The Pipeline, continued
1.text: The Pipeline, continued. Offline half (ingest to index) and online half (retrieve to answer) fail differently; separate their monitoring. Diagnose from the symptom: confident wrong answers after a document refresh, with model and latency unchanged, point first to retrieval or indexing (stale, missing or mismatched chunks), not to the model. Exam tip: When quality drops after a data refresh and the model is unchanged, investigate the retrieval and indexing step first.

1.title: Chunking
1.text: Chunking. The figure shows this: Chunking strategies: fixed size with overlap, structure-aware by headings, semantic by topic shift, and hierarchical parent and child chunks.

1.title: Chunking, continued
1.text: Chunking, continued. Fixed size with overlap. How: Equal token windows, small overlap. Best for: Uniform text; baseline. Risk: Cuts clauses and tables in half. Structure-aware. How: Split on headings, sections, clauses, rows. Best for: Regulations, manuals, code. Risk: Uneven sizes. Semantic. How: Split where topics change. Best for: Narrative text. Risk: Extra processing. Hierarchical (parent-child). How: Retrieve small chunks, return the larger parent. Best for: Precision plus context. Risk: More storage and logic. Special handling. How: Tables, code, lists kept intact. Best for: Structured content. Risk: Parser effort. Chunks are usually no more than a few hundred tokens; size, boundaries and overlap all change retrieval quality. Test sizes on your data.

1.title: Chunking, continued
1.text: Chunking, continued. Too large: relevance is diluted and context is wasted. Too small: meaning is lost ("the fee is two percent" without whose fee). Keep units whole: a clause, a table with its header, a function. Store metadata: source, section path, date, version, access group, language. Metadata enables filtering and citations.

1.title: Indexing
1.text: Indexing. Embeddings. Anthropic offers no embedding model; use a provider such as Voyage A I (general, multilingual, code, finance, law, multimodal, contextualized chunk models) and evaluate vendors on your data. Query versus document. Embed with the right input type (query or document) for retrieval. Similarity. Normalized vectors: cosine equals dot product. Dimension and quantization. Smaller dimensions or int eight or binary quantization cut storage (four times to thirty-two times) with some accuracy cost. Vector index. Fast approximate nearest-neighbor search over embeddings. Keyword index (B M twenty-five). Lexical ranking; strong for exact identifiers, codes, names. Hybrid. Combine vector and B M twenty-five scores; best general default.

1.title: Indexing, continued
1.text: Indexing, continued. Domain models. Legal, finance, code embeddings help specialized corpora.

1.title: Contextual retrieval
1.text: Contextual retrieval. The figure shows this: Contextual retrieval: prepend fifty to one hundred tokens of chunk-specific context before embedding and B M twenty-five indexing; combine with reranking for the lowest failure rate. A chunk like "the fee rose three percent" loses meaning out of context. Contextual retrieval has Claude write fifty to one hundred tokens of document-level context for each chunk and prepend it before embedding and before the B M twenty-five index.

1.title: Contextual retrieval, continued
1.text: Contextual retrieval, continued. Reported results (failure rate equals one minus recall@twenty, baseline five point seven percent): contextual embeddings -thirty-five percent; with contextual B M twenty-five -forty-nine percent; with reranking -sixty-seven percent. Prompt caching makes this cheap: load the document once and reference it for every chunk. Rerank: retrieve a larger candidate set (for example one hundred fifty), rerank, pass the top K (for example twenty) to the model; more chunks help up to a point, then distract. Reranking adds some latency.

1.title: Freshness, Security and Evaluation
1.text: Freshness, Security and Evaluation. Freshness. Incremental re-indexing; version documents; delete removed content; re-embed when the embedding model changes (never mix spaces); validate after each refresh. Access control. Store access metadata; filter retrieval by the user's permissions (Module eight). Prompt injection. Retrieved text is untrusted data: tag it, state that, limit tool power. Citations. Return source and location; verify that quoted text exists. Evaluation. Measure retrieval (recall@k, precision) separately from generation (faithfulness, correctness). Monitoring. Index age, empty-result rate, rerank scores, citation validity.

1.title: When not to use RAG
1.text: When not to use R A G. If the knowledge base is under about two hundred thousand tokens (roughly five hundred pages), consider putting it in the prompt with caching instead. Use R A G when the corpus is larger, changes often, or needs per-user access filtering and citations to sources. Exam tip: Quality drops after a data or embedding change with the model unchanged: check retrieval and indexing first. Exam tip: Under about two hundred thousand tokens, a cached prompt may beat building R A G.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Pipeline: Ingest, clean, chunk, enrich, embed and index, retrieve, rerank, generate with citations. Diagnose: Wrong answers after a refresh: check retrieval and index first. Chunks: A few hundred tokens; keep units whole; metadata for filtering and citation. Strategies: Fixed with overlap, structure-aware, semantic, hierarchical. Index: Vector plus B M twenty-five (hybrid); embed with the right input type; no Anthropic embedding model. Contextual retrieval: fifty to one hundred tokens of context; failure -thirty-five percent, -forty-nine percent, -sixty-seven percent with B M twenty-five and rerank. Rerank: Retrieve about one hundred fifty, pass top twenty. No R A G: Under about two hundred thousand tokens: cached prompt. Freshness: Incremental re-index; re-embed on model change; filter by access.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. After a team switches to a new embedding provider, a support assistant starts citing passages about the wrong products. Prompts, model and latency are unchanged, and the ingestion jobs report success. What should the architect check first? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Vectors from different embedding models are incompatible, so retrieval returns poor matches while everything else looks healthy.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Exact statute numbers and clause identifiers are being missed by an embeddings-only retriever. What is the best improvement? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Lexical search catches exact identifiers that embeddings can miss.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Chunks such as "the fee increased by three percent" retrieve poorly because the surrounding context is lost. Which technique addresses this directly? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A short, document-level context line prepended before embedding and keyword indexing restores the meaning that the chunk lost.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A corpus of sixty thousand tokens changes monthly and has no per-user access rules. What is a reasonable design? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Below about two hundred thousand tokens, a cached prompt can be simpler and faster.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Select two. Which two are required when the embedding model is replaced? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and C. Vectors from different models are incompatible; validate before switching.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A table in a P D F is split between two chunks and answers about it are wrong. What is the best fix? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Structure-aware chunking keeps a table together with its header, so retrieval returns the whole table instead of a fragment.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Which design lets the system return precise passages while still giving the model enough context? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Retrieving small child chunks and returning their larger parent balances precision with the context the model needs.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. A user-specific restriction must hold in a R A G system. Where should it be enforced? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Enforce access in code before the model sees data.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all eight answers. Question one: A. Question two: D. Question three: C. Question four: A. Question five: B and C. Question six: A. Question seven: C. Question eight: A. In the next module, we continue the course.
